doc_title: Polybenzimidazole-Derived and Non-Fluorinated Hydrocarbon Membranes for Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries: Structure–Property–Performance Relationships

gold_efus.evidence_text: The pristine PBI membrane exhibited the lowest ion exchange capacity of 1.2 mmol/g, consistent with its non-sulfonated aromatic structure where proton transport relies primarily on the intrinsic imidazole groups and absorbed acid within the membrane matrix.

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane, synthesized through controlled sulfonation of naphthyl-substituted PBI, achieved an ion exchange capacity of 1.42 mmol/g—representing a moderate increase of 18.3% relative to the unmodified PBI.
The SPEEK/APK composite membrane, prepared by blending sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone) with an amino-phenyl ketone crosslinker, displayed an intermediate ion exchange capacity of 1.8 mmol/g.

The SPTPC-2.59 membrane, featuring a densely sulfonated triphenyl-containing poly(arylene ether) backbone with the highest degree of sulfonation among the four materials, exhibited the highest ion exchange capacity of 2.59 mmol/g—more than double that of the pristine PBI.

gold_efus.condition: measured in 2.0 M H₂SO₄ at room temperature
gold_efus.evidence_text: The pristine PBI displayed the highest area resistance of 2.85 Ω·cm², reflecting the limited density of proton-conducting functional groups within its dense aromatic matrix.

gold_efus.condition: measured in 2.0 M H₂SO₄ at room temperature
gold_efus.evidence_text: The SNPBI-1.42 membrane demonstrated a substantially reduced area resistance of 1.42 Ω·cm²—exactly half the value measured for pristine PBI—indicating that the introduction of sulfonic acid groups on the naphthyl substituents significantly enhanced proton transport while preserving the overall chain rigidity.

gold_efus.condition: measured in 2.0 M H₂SO₄ at room temperature
gold_efus.evidence_text: The SPTPC-2.59 membrane achieved the lowest area resistance of 0.31 Ω·cm², representing a 9.2-fold reduction compared to the unmodified PBI.
The pristine PBI exhibited the lowest swelling ratio of 3.2%, consistent with its highly rigid backbone structure and extensive interchain hydrogen bonding.

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane showed a modestly increased swelling ratio of 5.8%, suggesting that the naphthyl sulfonation preserved the overall structural compactness despite the introduction of additional hydrophilic sulfonic acid groups.
The SPTPC-2.59 membrane exhibited the highest swelling ratio of 18.7%, which was 5.8 times greater than that of the pristine PBI.

gold_efus.condition: diaphragm diffusion cell with 1.5 M VOSO₄ in 3.0 M H₂SO₄ as feed
gold_efus.evidence_text: The pristine PBI demonstrated the lowest vanadium permeability of 0.8 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s, underscoring the exceptional ion-blocking capability of its densely packed aromatic structure.

gold_efus.condition: diaphragm diffusion cell with 1.5 M VOSO₄ in 3.0 M H₂SO₄ as feed
gold_efus.evidence_text: The SNPBI-1.42 membrane exhibited a slightly elevated vanadium permeability of 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s, representing a 50% increase relative to the unmodified PBI but maintaining a highly selective barrier.

gold_efus.condition: diaphragm diffusion cell with 1.5 M VOSO₄ in 3.0 M H₂SO₄ as feed
gold_efus.evidence_text: The SPTPC-2.59 membrane displayed the highest vanadium permeability of 8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s, exceeding that of the pristine PBI by more than one order of magnitude.
At a current density of 80 mA/cm², the pristine PBI membrane achieved a Coulombic efficiency of 98.6%, a voltage efficiency of 83.6%, and an energy efficiency of 82.4%.
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane demonstrated a Coulombic efficiency of 97.8%, a voltage efficiency of 93.3%, and an energy efficiency of 91.2% at the same 80 mA/cm² current density.

The SPTPC-2.59 membrane, despite possessing the lowest area resistance, exhibited the lowest Coulombic efficiency of 92.1% and a voltage efficiency of 95.1%, yielding an energy efficiency of 87.6% at 80 mA/cm².

The slight decrease in Coulombic efficiency relative to pristine PBI (by 0.8 percentage points) was accompanied by a substantial improvement in voltage efficiency (by 9.7 percentage points), resulting in a net gain of 8.8 percentage points in energy efficiency.

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane demonstrated superior capacity retention, with the initial discharge capacity of 1320 mAh decreasing to 1221 mAh after 500 cycles, yielding a capacity retention of 92.5% and the lowest fade rate among all tested membranes at 0.012% per cycle.

The SPTPC-2.59 membrane exhibited the poorest long-term capacity retention, with the initial discharge capacity of 1340 mAh falling to 1132 mAh over 500 cycles, representing a capacity retention of only 84.5% and the highest fade rate of 0.031% per cycle.

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane retained 96.3% of its initial ion exchange capacity after cycling, compared to 89.7% for the pristine PBI, 93.1% for the SPEEK/APK composite, and 84.2% for the SPTPC-2.59 membrane.

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane retained 96.3% of its initial ion exchange capacity after cycling, compared to 89.7% for the pristine PBI, 93.1% for the SPEEK/APK composite, and 84.2% for the SPTPC-2.59 membrane.

gold_efus.value: vanadium crossover and mechanical fatigue from swelling
gold_efus.evidence_text: In the SPTPC-2.59 membrane, the rapid capacity fade of 0.031% per cycle is attributed primarily to the substantial vanadium crossover (8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s), which leads to progressive electrolyte imbalance, accumulation of vanadium species in the opposing half-cell, and accelerated self-discharge reactions that compromise the long-term capacity. The elevated swelling ratio of 18.7% in this membrane may also contribute to gradual mechanical degradation and the formation of microscopic defects that further exacerbate vanadium permeation over extended cycling.

gold_efus.value: oxidative degradation of imidazole rings by VO₂⁺ species
gold_efus.evidence_text: In the pristine PBI membrane, the capacity fade rate of 0.028% per cycle, despite the lowest vanadium permeability, is associated with the progressive oxidative degradation of the imidazole rings by VO₂⁺ species, which gradually reduces the proton conductivity and increases the polarization losses over hundreds of cycles.

gold_efus.value: new carbonyl absorption bands at 1720 cm⁻¹
gold_efus.evidence_text: Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy of the cycled membranes indicated the appearance of new carbonyl absorption bands at 1720 cm⁻¹ in the pristine PBI and SPTPC-2.59 samples, consistent with oxidative cleavage of the aromatic ether linkages, while the SNPBI-1.42 membrane showed minimal changes in its infrared signature after 500 cycles.
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane achieves the highest energy efficiency of 91.2% at 80 mA/cm², outperforming both the pristine PBI (82.4%) and the SPTPC-2.59 (87.6%) at the same current density.

The SPEEK/APK composite membrane showed an initial discharge capacity of 1285 mAh declining to 1172 mAh after 500 cycles, corresponding to a capacity retention of 91.2% and a fade rate of 0.018% per cycle.
At the highest tested current density of 200 mA/cm², the energy efficiency values reached 72.5%, 83.2%, 78.6%, and 75.8% for PBI, SNPBI-1.42, SPEEK/APK, and SPTPC-2.59, respectively.

The optimal ion exchange capacity range for non-fluorinated membranes appears to fall between 1.3 and 1.6 mmol/g, where the balance between proton transport efficiency and vanadium selectivity is most favorable.
The swelling ratio serves as a practical indicator of long-term mechanical stability and should be maintained below approximately 8% for membranes intended for extended VRFB operation.
At 40 mA/cm², the energy efficiency values were 85.1%, 93.6%, 93.2%, and 91.4% for PBI, SNPBI-1.42, SPEEK/APK, and SPTPC-2.59, respectively.
As the current density increased to 120 mA/cm², the energy efficiency values decreased to 80.3%, 89.4%, 87.1%, and 84.2%, respectively.
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane demonstrated a Coulombic efficiency of 97.8%, a voltage efficiency of 93.3%, and an energy efficiency of 91.2% at the same 80 mA/cm² current density.

gold_facts.fact_statement: The pristine PBI membrane has an ion exchange capacity of 1.2 mmol/g.
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane has an ion exchange capacity of 1.42 mmol/g, which is 18.3% higher than pristine PBI.
The SPTPC-2.59 membrane has the highest IEC (2.59 mmol/g) among the four tested membranes, more than double that of pristine PBI.
The area resistance of PBI (2.85 Ω·cm²) is 9.2 times higher than that of SPTPC-2.59 (0.31 Ω·cm²).
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane has exactly half the area resistance of pristine PBI (1.42 vs 2.85 Ω·cm²).
The swelling ratio of SPTPC-2.59 (18.7%) is 5.8 times greater than that of pristine PBI (3.2%).
The vanadium permeability of SPTPC-2.59 (8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) exceeds that of pristine PBI (0.8 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) by more than one order of magnitude.
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane achieves the highest energy efficiency (91.2%) at 80 mA/cm² among all tested membranes.

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane gains 8.8 percentage points in energy efficiency over pristine PBI at 80 mA/cm² due to a 9.7 percentage point improvement in voltage efficiency that outweighs a 0.8 percentage point Coulombic efficiency loss.
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane has the lowest capacity fade rate (0.012% per cycle) over 500 cycles at 80 mA/cm².
The SPTPC-2.59 membrane has the highest capacity fade rate (0.031% per cycle) despite having the lowest area resistance, indicating that low resistance does not guarantee good cycling stability.
The capacity fade rate ranking from lowest to highest is: SNPBI-1.42 (0.012%) < SPEEK/APK (0.018%) < PBI (0.028%) < SPTPC-2.59 (0.031%) per cycle at 80 mA/cm².
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane retained 96.3% of its initial IEC after 500 cycles, which is higher than PBI (89.7%), SPEEK/APK (93.1%), and SPTPC-2.59 (84.2%).

The rapid capacity fade of SPTPC-2.59 is attributed primarily to substantial vanadium crossover (8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) leading to progressive electrolyte imbalance and self-discharge, with elevated swelling (18.7%) contributing to mechanical degradation.
Pristine PBI's capacity fade (0.028% per cycle) is caused by oxidative degradation of imidazole rings by VO₂⁺ species, not by vanadium crossover.

FTIR analysis showed new carbonyl absorption bands at 1720 cm⁻¹ in cycled PBI and SPTPC-2.59 membranes, consistent with oxidative cleavage of aromatic ether linkages, while SNPBI-1.42 showed minimal changes.
At 80 mA/cm², the energy efficiency ranking is SNPBI-1.42 (91.2%) > SPEEK/APK (90.4%) > SPTPC-2.59 (87.6%) > PBI (82.4%).
The SNPBI-1.42 membrane exhibits the most gradual decline in energy efficiency (10.4 percentage points) from 40 to 200 mA/cm², compared to PBI (12.6 pp) and SPTPC-2.59 (15.6 pp).
The optimal IEC range for non-fluorinated VRFB membranes is 1.3–1.6 mmol/g, as higher values increase vanadium permeability and lower values increase ohmic losses.

Long-term cycling stability correlates more strongly with membrane swelling behavior than with any single transport parameter, and the swelling ratio should be maintained below approximately 8% for extended VRFB operation.
The vanadium permeability of SNPBI-1.42 (1.2 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) is 50% higher than pristine PBI (0.8 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) but represents only 14% of the SPTPC-2.59 value (8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s).

The SNPBI-1.42 membrane outperforms all other membranes across all tested current densities (40–200 mA/cm²) in terms of energy efficiency, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at intermediate to high current densities (80–160 mA/cm²).

The Coulombic efficiency of pristine PBI (98.6%) is higher than SNPBI-1.42 (97.8%), SPEEK/APK (95.4%), and SPTPC-2.59 (92.1%) at 80 mA/cm², demonstrating that lower IEC generally yields higher Coulombic efficiency.

The rigid backbone modification strategy (SNPBI-1.42) outperforms both the polymer blending approach (SPEEK/APK) and the high-degree sulfonation approach (SPTPC-2.59) in terms of energy efficiency and cycling stability.

Increasing IEC from 1.42 to 2.59 mmol/g reduces area resistance by 9.2× (from 1.42 to 0.31 Ω·cm²) but increases vanadium permeability by 7.1× (from 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ to 8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s), demonstrating a fundamental conductivity–selectivity trade-off in non-fluorinated membranes.

qa_pairs.question: What is the ion exchange capacity of the SNPBI-1.42 membrane?
qa_pairs.answer: 1.42 mmol/g

qa_pairs.question: What is the area resistance of pristine PBI measured in 2.0 M H₂SO₄?
qa_pairs.answer: 2.85 Ω·cm²

qa_pairs.question: Which membrane achieves the highest energy efficiency at 80 mA/cm²?
qa_pairs.answer: SNPBI-1.42 membrane, with 91.2% energy efficiency.

qa_pairs.question: What is the capacity fade rate of the SPTPC-2.59 membrane over 500 cycles at 80 mA/cm²?
qa_pairs.answer: 0.031% per cycle

qa_pairs.question: What is the vanadium permeability of the SNPBI-1.42 membrane?
How does the SNPBI-1.42 membrane achieve higher energy efficiency than pristine PBI despite slightly lower Coulombic efficiency?
qa_pairs.answer: The SNPBI-1.42 membrane gains 8.8 percentage points in energy efficiency because its voltage efficiency improves by 9.7 percentage points (from 83.6% to 93.3% at 80 mA/cm²), which far outweighs the small 0.8 percentage point decrease in Coulombic efficiency (from 98.6% to 97.8%). The reduced area resistance (1.42 vs 2.85 Ω·cm²) is the primary driver of the voltage efficiency improvement.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the SPTPC-2.59 membrane, despite having the lowest area resistance, exhibit the highest capacity fade rate?
qa_pairs.answer: The SPTPC-2.59 membrane's rapid capacity fade (0.031% per cycle) is attributed to two primary factors: (1) its high vanadium permeability (8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) causes progressive electrolyte imbalance and accelerated self-discharge, and (2) its high swelling ratio (18.7%) leads to mechanical degradation and microscopic defect formation over extended cycling. Additionally, it showed the lowest post-cycling IEC retention (84.2%), indicating chemical degradation of sulfonic acid groups.

qa_pairs.question: What is the energy efficiency ranking of all four membranes at 80 mA/cm²?
What causes the capacity fade in pristine PBI membrane since it has the lowest vanadium permeability?
qa_pairs.answer: Pristine PBI's capacity fade (0.028% per cycle) is caused by progressive oxidative degradation of the imidazole rings by VO₂⁺ species in the charged positive electrolyte, which gradually reduces proton conductivity and increases polarization losses. This was confirmed by FTIR analysis showing new carbonyl absorption bands at 1720 cm⁻¹ after 500 cycles, consistent with oxidative cleavage of aromatic ether linkages.

qa_pairs.question: What is the optimal IEC range for non-fluorinated VRFB membranes according to this study?
qa_pairs.answer: 1.3 to 1.6 mmol/g. Membranes with IEC below this range suffer from excessive ohmic losses, while membranes with IEC above this range experience unacceptable vanadium crossover.

qa_pairs.question: How does the SNPBI-1.42 membrane's energy efficiency change from 40 to 200 mA/cm²?
qa_pairs.answer: The SNPBI-1.42 membrane's energy efficiency decreases from 93.6% at 40 mA/cm² to 83.2% at 200 mA/cm², a decline of 10.4 percentage points. This is the most gradual decline among all tested membranes.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the SNPBI-1.42 membrane outperform SPTPC-2.59 despite having lower proton conductivity (higher area resistance)?
qa_pairs.answer: The SNPBI-1.42 membrane outperforms SPTPC-2.59 because VRFB performance depends on the balance between proton transport and vanadium selectivity, not just conductivity alone. At 80 mA/cm², SNPBI-1.42's Coulombic efficiency (97.8%) is 5.7 percentage points higher than SPTPC-2.59 (92.1%), which more than compensates for its 1.8 percentage point lower voltage efficiency (93.3% vs 95.1%). The rigid PBI backbone provides better vanadium blocking (1.2 vs 8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) and lower swelling (5.8% vs 18.7%), leading to better long-term stability (0.012% vs 0.031% fade rate).

qa_pairs.question: What is the relationship between membrane swelling ratio and long-term cycling stability?
qa_pairs.answer: Long-term cycling stability correlates more strongly with swelling ratio than with any single transport parameter. Membranes with swelling ratios below approximately 8% achieve superior durability. SNPBI-1.42 (5.8% swelling, 0.012% fade rate) significantly outperforms SPTPC-2.59 (18.7% swelling, 0.031% fade rate), suggesting that excessive dimensional changes during hydration–dehydration cycles cause mechanical fatigue and defect formation.

qa_pairs.question: What are the three architectural approaches to non-fluorinated VRFB membrane design compared in this study, and which performs best?
qa_pairs.answer: The three approaches are: (1) rigid backbone modification (PBI → SNPBI-1.42), (2) polymer blending (SPEEK/APK), and (3) high-degree sulfonation of flexible backbones (SPTPC-2.59). The rigid backbone modification strategy performs best, with SNPBI-1.42 achieving 91.2% energy efficiency at 80 mA/cm² and the lowest capacity fade rate of 0.012% per cycle, outperforming SPEEK/APK (90.4%, 0.018%) and SPTPC-2.59 (87.6%, 0.031%).

qa_pairs.question: How does increasing IEC from 1.42 to 2.59 mmol/g affect the trade-off between proton conductivity and vanadium selectivity?
qa_pairs.answer: Increasing IEC from 1.42 to 2.59 mmol/g reduces area resistance by 9.2× (from 1.42 to 0.31 Ω·cm²) but simultaneously increases vanadium permeability by 7.1× (from 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ to 8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s). This demonstrates a fundamental conductivity–selectivity trade-off: higher IEC improves proton transport but creates non-selective ionic channels that also transport vanadium ions. The optimal performance is achieved at intermediate IEC (1.3–1.6 mmol/g) where the balance is most favorable.

qa_pairs.question: What FTIR evidence supports the different degradation mechanisms for PBI and SNPBI-1.42 membranes?
qa_pairs.answer: After 500 cycles, FTIR showed new carbonyl absorption bands at 1720 cm⁻¹ in cycled PBI and SPTPC-2.59 samples, consistent with oxidative cleavage of aromatic ether linkages. In contrast, the SNPBI-1.42 membrane showed minimal changes in its infrared signature and retained 96.3% of its initial IEC, confirming that moderate sulfonation of PBI-type backbones does not compromise oxidative resistance.

qa_pairs.question: At what current density does the performance advantage of SNPBI-1.42 become most pronounced?
qa_pairs.answer: The SNPBI-1.42 membrane consistently maintains the highest energy efficiency across all tested current densities (40–200 mA/cm²), with the performance advantage becoming most pronounced at intermediate to high current densities of 80–160 mA/cm². At 80 mA/cm², its energy efficiency is 91.2% vs 82.4% for PBI and 87.6% for SPTPC-2.59.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Coulombic efficiency of pristine PBI at 80 mA/cm² and why is it higher than SPTPC-2.59?
qa_pairs.answer: Pristine PBI achieves 98.6% Coulombic efficiency at 80 mA/cm², compared to 92.1% for SPTPC-2.59. This difference arises because PBI's densely packed aromatic structure (swelling 3.2%, vanadium permeability 0.8 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s) provides superior vanadium blocking compared to SPTPC-2.59's highly swollen structure (swelling 18.7%, vanadium permeability 8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s). Lower IEC generally correlates with higher Coulombic efficiency.

qa_pairs.question: What is the capacity retention of SNPBI-1.42 after 500 cycles at 80 mA/cm²?
qa_pairs.answer: 92.5%, with initial discharge capacity of 1320 mAh declining to 1221 mAh.

qa_pairs.question: Why is maximum IEC not optimal for VRFB membrane performance?
qa_pairs.answer: Maximum IEC is not optimal because while it reduces area resistance (improving voltage efficiency), it simultaneously increases vanadium permeability (degrading Coulombic efficiency) and membrane swelling (reducing mechanical stability). The SPTPC-2.59 membrane has the highest IEC (2.59 mmol/g) and lowest resistance (0.31 Ω·cm²) but suffers from high vanadium permeability (8.5 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s), low Coulombic efficiency (92.1%), and the highest capacity fade rate (0.031%/cycle). The optimal IEC range of 1.3–1.6 mmol/g, exemplified by SNPBI-1.42 (1.42 mmol/g), balances these competing factors.

normalization_stress_points.note: The document distinguishes between 'pristine PBI'/'unmodified PBI' (IEC 1.2 mmol/g) and 'SNPBI-1.42' (IEC 1.42 mmol/g). Systems must not conflate these. PBI refers to the unsulfonated base polymer; SNPBI-1.42 is a chemically modified derivative with sulfonic acid groups on naphthyl substituents.

The SPEEK/APK composite membrane is referred to as both 'composite membrane' and 'blend membrane.' The SPTPC-2.59 membrane is described as a 'densely sulfonated triphenyl poly(arylene ether).' Systems must recognize these refer to specific materials, not generic membrane categories.

normalization_stress_points.description: IEC vs area resistance - values must be paired with correct membrane
normalization_stress_points.note: Critical bindings: PBI: IEC 1.2 mmol/g, resistance 2.85 Ω·cm²; SNPBI-1.42: IEC 1.42 mmol/g, resistance 1.42 Ω·cm²; SPEEK/APK: IEC 1.8 mmol/g, resistance 0.78 Ω·cm²; SPTPC-2.59: IEC 2.59 mmol/g, resistance 0.31 Ω·cm². The values 1.42 and 2.59 appear both as IEC values and as membrane identifiers in the names.

normalization_stress_points.description: Swelling ratio vs proton transport correlation
normalization_stress_points.note: Higher swelling does not directly indicate better proton transport for VRFB performance. SPTPC-2.59 has the highest swelling (18.7%) and lowest resistance (0.31 Ω·cm²) but underperforms SNPBI-1.42 (swelling 5.8%, resistance 1.42 Ω·cm²) in energy efficiency. Systems must recognize swelling as a mechanical stability indicator rather than a conductivity proxy.

The document uses 'non-fluorinated,' 'hydrocarbon,' and 'non-fluorinated hydrocarbon' interchangeably to describe the membrane class. 'PBI-derived' refers specifically to PBI and SNPBI-1.42, while 'non-fluorinated hydrocarbon' encompasses all four membranes including SPEEK/APK and SPTPC-2.59. Systems must distinguish between the broader category and the PBI subclass.

normalization_stress_points.description: Current density conditions must be preserved with efficiency values
normalization_stress_points.note: Efficiency values are strongly current-density dependent. For example, SNPBI-1.42 energy efficiency is 93.6% at 40 mA/cm², 91.2% at 80 mA/cm², 89.4% at 120 mA/cm², 86.7% at 160 mA/cm², and 83.2% at 200 mA/cm². Systems must not report efficiency values without specifying the current density.

normalization_stress_points.description: Capacity fade causes differ across membranes despite similar fade rates
normalization_stress_points.note: Pristine PBI (0.028%/cycle fade) and SPTPC-2.59 (0.031%/cycle fade) have similar fade rates but completely different causes: PBI fades due to oxidative degradation of imidazole rings by VO₂⁺, while SPTPC-2.59 fades due to vanadium crossover and mechanical degradation from swelling. Systems must not assume similar rates imply similar mechanisms.

normalization_stress_points.description: Vanadium permeability values share the 10⁻⁷ cm²/s scale
normalization_stress_points.note: All vanadium permeability values are expressed in the range of 10⁻⁷ cm²/s. PBI: 0.8, SNPBI-1.42: 1.2, SPEEK/APK: 3.6, SPTPC-2.59: 8.5 (all ×10⁻⁷ cm²/s). Systems must maintain this common scale factor when comparing or aggregating values.

normalization_stress_points.description: Post-cycling characterization applies only to 500-cycle test at 80 mA/cm²
normalization_stress_points.note: All post-cycling data (IEC retention, FTIR changes) refer specifically to the 500-cycle test conducted at 80 mA/cm². Systems must not generalize these results to other current densities or cycle counts. SNPBI-1.42 retained 96.3% IEC; PBI 89.7%; SPEEK/APK 93.1%; SPTPC-2.59 84.2%.

normalization_stress_points.description: Percentage point differences vs relative percentage changes
normalization_stress_points.note: The document uses both percentage point differences (e.g., SNPBI-1.42 gains 8.8 percentage points over PBI in energy efficiency) and relative percentage changes (e.g., SNPBI-1.42 IEC is 18.3% higher than PBI). Systems must distinguish between these: 8.8 pp means (91.2 - 82.4) = 8.8, while 18.3% means (1.42 - 1.20) / 1.20 × 100 = 18.3%.
